problem: Outdoor VLN (Touchdown) suffers from scarce human-annotated instructions; Speaker-based back-translation hallucinates on complex street views, and template instructions from Google Maps API (street names and directions) differ in style from human instructions that refer to visual objects, so they cannot be fully used.
motivation: Outdoor trajectories are long and visually diverse, so agents need object-rich instructions, but human annotation is expensive. Cheap Google Maps/StreetLearn routes exist but are stylistically mismatched, so converting their style could turn them into useful pre-training data.
key_idea: Train a masking-and-recovering multimodal style transfer model (Speaker plus textual attention over a masked instruction skeleton) to rewrite template StreetLearn instructions into object-grounded human-like style, then pre-train a Transformer navigator on them before fine-tuning on Touchdown.
insight: Style transfer conditioned on both the trajectory and the template skeleton preserves guiding signals while adding visual objects. The ablation shows that Speaker-generated instructions hurt (TC 15.5 to 8.3 on test) and Speaker+text attention also hurts (11.8), whereas MTST helps (16.2), so the skeleton and the visual grounding both matter. Instruction quality metrics track this: MTST achieves MR 46.7 vs 8.3 for the Speaker.
method: Masking-and-recovering: with NLTK POS tags, mask object tokens in human Touchdown instructions (training) or street names in Google Maps instructions (inference), keeping direction cues like 'turn left', and train the model to recover the full instruction.

Multimodal style transfer model: Speaker-based LSTM encoder-decoder with visual soft attention over 8 ResNet18 panorama slices and additional textual soft attention over sentence embeddings of the masked skeleton; cross-entropy with teacher forcing.
Manh-50 auxiliary dataset: 31k StreetLearn Manhattan trajectories with at most 50 panoramas, whose instructions are rewritten by the style transfer model.
VLN Transformer instruction encoder: BERT-base per-sentence mean-pooled embeddings projected by FC to 256-d (sentence-level splitting; the appendix ablation shows split TC 13.6 vs no split 9.6).
View encoder: panorama sliced into 8 views, ResNet18 features, centered on heading and cropped, then a 3-layer CNN gives a 256-d feature per step.

Cross-modal encoder and action predictor: 8-layer, 8-head, 256-d Transformer over sentence and view tokens with a causal mask over future views, segment and position embeddings, and an FC action head (left/right/forward/stop) with cross-entropy.
Two-stage training: pre-train on Manh-50 with stylized instructions, then fine-tune on Touchdown; the approach is also applied to RCONCAT and GA baselines.

setting.backbone: VLN Transformer (BERT-base + ResNet18 + 8-layer Transformer, trained; BERT fine-tuned); style transfer model is an LSTM Speaker with textual attention
setting.training_data: Touchdown train (6,526 samples); pre-training on Manh-50 (31k StreetLearn Manhattan samples) with stylized instructions; the style model is trained on Touchdown instructions
setting.observation: Street View panoramas (8 perspective slices, ResNet18 features) plus heading
setting.action_space: discrete: turn left, turn right, go forward, stop, on the Street View graph

numbers_note: Touchdown is not in the canonical benchmark list, so it is labelled other:Touchdown; the dev set is labelled 'val'. Relative improvement of 8.7% is TC 16.2 vs 14.9 on the test set.
results: On Touchdown test, the VLN Transformer with MTST pre-training reaches TC 16.2 and SDTW 15.0, versus 14.9 and 14.0 without pre-training (8.7% relative TC gain), and beats RCONCAT (11.8) and GA (11.9). Style-modified pre-training improves over vanilla Manh-50 pre-training on RCONCAT, GA and the VLN Transformer alike. MTST also gives the best instruction quality (BLEU 30.6, MR 46.7) and wins the human evaluation.
limitations: Absolute task completion remains low (about 16%), and SPD/CLS are worse than the LSTM baseline GA because the agent takes longer paths in failure cases.
The pipeline is two-stage rather than end-to-end, and the alignment between generated instructions and trajectories is not quantitatively evaluated.
Style-modified instructions can still contain errors, and gains are modest (about 1 TC point).
